title: Cheerleader Effect (Group Attractiveness)
description: Faces appear more attractive when seen in a group than when viewed in isolation. The group averages out individual flaws.

sections.title: What It Is
sections.content: Faces appear more attractive when seen in a group than when viewed in isolation. The group averages out individual flaws.

sections.title: How It Actually Appears
content: A person you barely noticed in a crowd photo suddenly looks less striking when you see their solo picture.
Friend groups collectively appear more attractive than the sum of their individual photos.
In a bar, someone who seemed appealing within a group of friends seems less so when approached alone, and vice versa.

sections.title: Common Behaviors
content: Being more impressed by a group’s overall appeal.
Feeling disappointed when a date shows up alone and doesn’t match the group impression.
Using group photos on dating apps to boost perceived attractiveness.

sections.title: Warning Signs
content: You can’t quite explain why someone looked better earlier, but the context changed.
You’re making snap judgments based on group imagery.
You find yourself more drawn to someone when they’re with friends than when they’re alone.

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: The visual system quickly computes an ensemble representation of a group, averaging facial features into a more prototypical—and thus often more attractive—composite. Walker & Vul (2014) demonstrated the effect experimentally: faces in groups were rated higher than the same faces individually.

sections.title: Protection Strategy
content: Evaluate people individually; don’t let group context inflate or deflate your impression.
If you notice a strong “group hotness” effect, look at each face separately and judge independently.
Be aware that the effect applies to you too; you might appear more attractive when out with friends.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
content: Assuming the effect means you shouldn’t go out in groups. It’s a perceptual bias, not a rule to manipulate social strategy.
Over-relying on group photos when assessing romantic prospects.

sections.title: Real Scenario
sections.content: A man sees a group photo of a woman with her friends and is very attracted. On their first solo date, he’s surprised that the attraction is less intense—not because she looks different, but because the cheerleader effect inflated his initial perception.

sections.title: Key Insight
sections.content: A group is a beauty filter. Before you zoom in, remember that the lens may be flattering more than the face.
